Programming Paradigms · session 10 · demo of block 1

A type checker for mini-ML

The file mini_ml_typing.ml is the demo of the lecture's first block: a type checker for mini-ML, a small functional language, here monomorphic and with the parameter of every function annotated. The slides of block 1 show the same code; this page adds the explanations that the file carries in its comments, and the ways to run it.

How to run it

Each way below starts in a terminal, in the folder that holds mini_ml_typing.ml.

The whole file, from the shell

The toplevel reads the file one phrase after the other and prints an answer for each: the definitions, then the 4 types of the well-typed tests, then the 3 exceptions of the ill-typed ones. Read this way, the toplevel goes on after an exception, so all 7 tests run.

Before each answer the toplevel also prints its prompt, a #, followed by one * for each line of comment it has read; the listing leaves those characters out, and it folds the signature of Smap (48 lines, the operations of Map.Make) into sig ... end.

The file loaded in the toplevel

The command ocaml alone opens the toplevel; the directive #use then loads the file. The first # is the prompt, the second belongs to the directive.

#use stops at the first exception that nothing catches: the 4 types and the first failure appear, and the 2 tests after it do not run. The definitions made before the exception stay, so each remaining test runs when its phrase is pasted at the prompt:

An expression typed by hand

After #use, typeof accepts any value of type expression. The mini-ML function fun x:int -> (x, x) is written with the constructors, and the toplevel answers with its type, int -> int * int, as a value of type typ:

OCaml version and libraries

The outputs on this page come from The OCaml toplevel, version 5.4.0. The file uses the standard library only (Map, String, failwith): no package and no build step are needed.

Monomorphic mini-ML

mini-ML here is monomorphic: every expression has at most one type, and no type contains a type variable. The parameter of every function carries a type annotation written by the programmer, as in

With that annotation, the checker never has to guess a type: it computes the type of each expression from the types of its parts, bottom up.

Types

The types of mini-ML.

typ is a variant type: a value of type typ is built by exactly one of the constructors below. A constructor with of carries arguments; a constructor without of is a constant. The definition is recursive: Tarrow and Tproduct contain smaller types.

Example: the type (int * int) -> int of the operator + is the value

ConstructorMeaning
TintThe type int.
Tarrow of typ * typTarrow (t1, t2) is the type t1 -> t2: the functions from t1 to t2.
Tproduct of typ * typTproduct (t1, t2) is the type t1 * t2: the pairs of a t1 and a t2.

Expressions

The abstract syntax tree of mini-ML, the same as for the evaluator, except for Fun. Each constructor below comes with the concrete syntax it stands for.

The operator + takes one argument, a pair: the concrete syntax +(x, 1) is the application

Why Fun carries a type and Let does not. In let x = e1 in e2 the expression e1 is there: the checker computes its type, and that type is the type of x. In fun x -> e nothing in the expression says what x will be bound to: the argument arrives later, at an application that may be anywhere else in the program. A monomorphic checker that works bottom up therefore needs the type of x written down. Type inference (the next step of the course) removes this annotation.

ConstructorMeaning
Var of stringVar "x" is the variable x.
Const of intConst 3 is the integer constant 3.
Op of stringOp "+" is the primitive operator +.
Fun of string * typ * expressionFun ("x", Tint, e) is the function fun x:int -> e, whose parameter x has type int. The type is the only change from the syntax tree of the evaluator.
App of expression * expressionApp (e1, e2) is e1 e2, the application of e1 to the argument e2.
Pair of expression * expressionPair (e1, e2) is the pair (e1, e2).
Let of string * expression * expressionLet ("x", e1, e2) is the local definition let x = e1 in e2.

Typing environments

The module Smap

Maps whose keys are strings.

Map.Make is a functor: a function from modules to modules. Applied to the module String (which provides the type string and a comparison compare on it), it returns a module of maps whose keys are strings. That module is named Smap.

Smap.t is the type of those maps, parameterized by the type of the values: typ Smap.t is the type of maps from strings to types.

The maps of Map.Make are persistent, like the data structures of session 2: Smap.add x ty env returns a new map, with x bound to ty, and leaves env unchanged. A binding of x already present in env is hidden in the new map only.

Smap.find x env returns the value bound to x in env, and raises the exception Not_found when x is not bound.

The type env

An environment, written Gamma in the typing rules, maps each variable in scope to its type: it is a map from string to typ.

The type checker

The function type_expr

type_expr env e returns the type of e in the environment env, that is, the type tau such that the judgment

holds, with Gamma = env. When no such type exists, the function raises an exception.

The keyword function introduces an anonymous function of one argument that is matched at once against the patterns that follow. The definition

is the same as

There is one case per constructor of expression, and each case implements one typing rule. A rule is written with its premises above the line and its conclusion below.

failwith msg raises the exception Failure msg; it is how the checker reports a type error.

Where the checks are. The cases for constants, variables, operators, functions, pairs and let never compare two types: each one builds the type of the expression from the types of its parts, and any type of the parts is acceptable. Only an application constrains its parts: e1 must be a function, and the type of e2 must be the type of its parameter. So the application case is the only place where the checker detects a mismatch of types. Two other failures are not mismatches: an unbound variable (Not_found, raised by Smap.find) and an unknown operator (the failwith of the Op op case).

The cases of type_expr

The function opens with the line below; its cases follow, each with the typing rule it implements, in the order of the file.

Case Const _rule (const)

Case Var xrule (var)

Smap.find raises Not_found when x is not in Gamma.

Case Op "+"rule (op+)

The pattern Op "+" matches only the string "+": a constant in a pattern is compared with the value. The patterns are tried in order, so every other operator falls to the next case.

Case Op opno rule

No rule for any other operator: the checker rejects it.

Case Fun (x, ty, e)rule (fun)

The body e is checked in Gamma extended with x:tau1. Smap.add builds that extended environment as a new map; env itself is not modified. This is exactly what the rule needs: x is in scope in the body only, and once the body is checked, the rest of the program still uses Gamma, in which x has its old type or no type at all.

Case Pair (e1, e2)rule (pair)

Case Let (x, e1, e2)rule (let)

The type tau1 of e1 is computed first, in Gamma, where x is not yet bound (the let is not recursive). Then e2 is checked in Gamma extended with x:tau1, again a new map built by Smap.add.

Case App (e1, e2)rule (app)

The two premises give the two checks: the type of e1 must be an arrow, and the type of e2 must be equal to the parameter type tau2 of that arrow.

begin match ... end delimits the inner match. Without it, the cases of the inner match would continue to the end of the outer function; here App is the last case, so the delimiters only make the extent of the inner match visible. The inner match tells an arrow type from any other type.

= is the structural equality of OCaml: two values of type typ are equal when they are built by the same constructors with equal arguments, all the way down. Two types written separately, such as Tarrow (Tint, Tint) and Tarrow (Tint, Tint), are therefore equal.

The function typeof

typeof e is the type of e in the empty environment: a closed expression has no free variables, so it needs no bindings. The definition is a partial application: type_expr receives its first argument, Smap.empty, and typeof is the function that waits for the expression.

Tests

Each test is a separate top-level phrase ending with ;;. In the toplevel, a well-typed test prints its type, and an ill-typed test prints the exception it raises.

The well-typed tests come first. ocaml < mini_ml_typing.ml runs every phrase, whatever exceptions the earlier ones raise. #use stops at the first uncaught exception: it prints the four types and the first failure, and the two other ill-typed tests are then pasted one by one.
